blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Part XIV-A was added to the Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976, introducing Articles 323A and 323B.
Article 323A empowers Parliament to establish Administrative Tribunals for disputes relating to public service recruitment and conditions.
Article 323B allows both Parliament and State Legislatures to create tribunals for specific matters like taxation, foreign exchange, and land reforms.
In the landmark L. Chandra Kumar case (1997), the Supreme Court ruled that judicial review by High Courts under Articles 226/227 cannot be excluded.
Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies guided by principles of natural justice rather than strict rules of the Civil Procedure Code.

blocks.content: Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies established to deal with specific types of disputes. They were created to reduce the burden on regular courts and to provide speedy justice in specialized matters.
Tribunals perform judicial as well as administrative functions and work under the supervision of the judiciary.
Tribunals were added to the Constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976. They are mentioned in:
Article 323A empowers Parliament to establish Administrative Tribunals for:

items:
• Service matters of central government employees
  • Disputes relating to recruitment and service conditions
Service matters of central government employees
Disputes relating to recruitment and service conditions

blocks.content: Under this article, the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was established in 1985.
The CAT deals with service matters of:

items:
• Central Government employees
  • Employees of Union Territories
  • Employees of public sector undertakings

• Headed by a Chairman
  • Benches across India
  • Decisions are subject to judicial review by High Court
Decisions are subject to judicial review by High Court

blocks.content: State Governments can establish State Administrative Tribunals for their employees. Features:

items:
• Created with approval of Parliament
  • Can be abolished later
  • Decisions are appealable in High Court
Decisions are appealable in High Court

blocks.content: Article 323B allows establishment of tribunals for matters like:

items:
• Taxation
  • Industrial disputes
  • Land reforms
  • Ceiling on urban property
  • Elections
  • Food procurement

• Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT)
  • National Green Tribunal (NGT)
  • National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)
  • National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission
  • Armed Forces Tribunal

blocks.content: In the L. Chandra Kumar case (1997), the Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review over the decisions of tribunals by High Courts under Article 226/227 is an essential feature of the basic structure of the Constitution.

items:

blocks.content: Tribunals play a vital role in:

items:
• Speedy justice delivery
  • Reducing pendency of courts
  • Specialized dispute resolution
Article 323A tribunals can be established ONLY by Parliament, whereas Article 323B tribunals can be established by both Parliament and State Legislatures within their competence.
Direct appeals from CAT to the Supreme Court under Article 136 are no longer permissible as a first step; appeals must first go before the Division Bench of the concerned High Court.
Unlike traditional courts, tribunals consist of both judicial members and expert technical/administrative members.

• Constitutional limits
  • Principles of natural justice
  • Judicial review of higher courts

• Tribunal Reforms Act, 2021
  • Reduction in number of tribunals
  • Uniform tenure of members

blocks.content: Tribunals are an essential part of the Indian judicial system. They provide speedy and expert justice in specialized matters.
However, proper reforms and independence are necessary to ensure their effective functioning.
